title: Yellow eyes in a 30-year-old woman back from Thailand
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 30-year-old interior designer in general practice. Her partner noticed yesterday that her eyes look yellow. She has had two weeks of feeling hot, poor appetite, malaise, right upper quadrant pain, dark urine, pale stools, itch and nausea, and she came back from Thailand a month ago without any pre-travel vaccines. The candidate then interprets her hepatitis serology, liver function tests and abdominal ultrasound, recognises acute hepatitis A in a patient who is vaccine-immune to hepatitis B, and plans supportive care, public health notification, protection of her partner, monitoring and safety netting.
focus: Jaundice in a returned traveller: the 4 Ps, hepatitis and travel risk factors, and reading hepatitis serology and liver tests
stem: You are a medical student on placement at a metropolitan general practice. Sanjana Kumar, a 30-year-old woman, has come to the clinic because her eyes have turned yellow. Your supervising GP has asked you to see her first.
tasks: Take a focused history from Sanjana and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Sanjana's hepatitis serology, blood tests and abdominal ultrasound report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Sanjana Kumar, a 30-year-old interior designer. You are polite and cooperative but scared, because nothing like this has ever happened to you. Answer only what you are asked. For anything not covered below, say "no" or "I don't know". The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I've been feeling a bit ill recently, which I thought was no big deal. But then yesterday my partner said my eyes looked a bit more yellow than usual, so I thought I should get this checked out."

The yellowing (give only when asked):

  • It is your eyes. You haven't noticed any change in your skin.
  • It came on gradually. Your partner first noticed it yesterday.
  • You haven't tried anything for it. It has never happened before.

Feeling unwell (only if asked):

  • "I haven't measured my temperature, but I've felt hot for the past two weeks."
  • You have gone off your food and felt generally unwell (malaise) for two weeks.
  • No weight loss, no night sweats.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • Pain in the right upper part of your tummy. It is constant and has nothing to do with eating.
  • Your poo has gone pale.
  • Your wee has gone dark.
  • You are itchy.
  • You feel sick (nauseated).
  • No vomiting, no change in your bowel habit, no blood in your poo.

Travel (only if asked):

  • You went to Thailand and came back a month ago.
  • If asked about food: you ate hotel food and street food.
  • If asked about water: you drank only bottled water.
  • If asked where you stayed: a hotel and a hostel.
  • If asked what you did: sightseeing, and you went swimming on the last day. You don't remember anything else about the swim.
  • If asked about vaccines: you had your childhood vaccines, but you didn't have any vaccines before the trip.

Other risk factors (say no if asked): injecting drugs, tattoos, piercings, blood transfusions or needlestick injuries. You don't drink alcohol. You have never had gallstones.

Sexual and menstrual history (only if asked): one long-term male partner, vaginal sex, and you always use condoms. Your period was last week. You have never had an STI screen.

Past medical history: asthma since you were 5. You have never had gallstones or cancer.

Medications: Ventolin (salbutamol) puffer. No recent changes. No other medicines, supplements or herbal remedies.

Allergies: none.

Family history: nothing relevant. No hepatitis, gallstones or cancer in the family.

Social history: non-smoker, no alcohol. You live with your boyfriend in an apartment in the city. You work as an interior designer. You were born in Australia.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: you have no idea what it could be.
  • Concern: "This has never happened to me before, so I'm quite scared."
  • Expectation: "I'd like to know what's going on."

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: alert and fully oriented, looks tired but not distressed. No bruising or petechiae. Weight 62 kg.
  • Observations: temperature 37.8 °C, HR 92 regular, BP 116/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, capillary BGL 5.2 mmol/L.
  • Jaundice: obvious scleral icterus. A faint yellow tinge to the skin in natural light. Scratch marks on both forearms.
  • Hydration: mucous membranes moist, CRT under 2 seconds.
  • Hands: no clubbing, leuconychia, palmar erythema or Dupuytren's contracture. No asterixis.
  • Face, neck and chest: no spider naevi. No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. No rash.
  • Chest and heart: chest clear. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs.
  • Abdomen: not distended, no scars. Tender in the right upper quadrant, with no guarding. Smooth, soft, tender liver edge palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin. Murphy's sign negative. Spleen not palpable. No masses. No shifting dullness. Bowel sounds normal.
  • Mental state: alert, oriented, no confusion.
  • Urine dipstick (if requested): bilirubin 2+, urobilinogen not increased. Blood, leucocytes, nitrites and protein negative.
  • Urine pregnancy test (if requested): negative.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Sanjana's identity and gains consent.
Uses plain language and responds with empathy to her fear that this has never happened before.
History
Characterises the jaundice:

kids.x: Site and onset: eyes only, no skin change noticed; came on gradually and her partner first noticed it yesterday.
First episode, and nothing tried for it.

check.x: Asks about the 4 Ps:

kids.x: Pee and poo: dark urine and pale stools.
kids.d: These point to conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, so they must be asked about directly.

kids.x: Pain: right upper quadrant, constant, not related to food.

check.x: Asks about constitutional symptoms: has felt hot for 2 weeks (not measured), with anorexia and malaise for 2 weeks; no weight loss or night sweats.
Asks about other gastrointestinal symptoms: nausea, with no vomiting, change in bowel habit or blood in the stool.

Asks questions exploring causes from all three groups: pre-hepatic (haemolysis, malaria, known blood disorders), hepatic (viral, alcohol, drugs, autoimmune) and post-hepatic (gallstones, pain after fatty food, weight loss or malignancy).
check.d: Award for at least one question in each of the three groups.

check.x: Asks about blood-borne and other hepatitis risk factors:

kids.x: Injecting drug use, tattoos, piercings, blood transfusions and needlestick injuries (none).
Sexual history: one long-term male partner, vaginal sex, always uses condoms, never had an STI screen.
Alcohol intake (none), and over-the-counter or herbal medicines (none).

check.x: Takes a returned-traveller history:

kids.x: Where and when: Thailand, back a month ago.
Food and water: hotel and street food, bottled water only.
Accommodation and activities: hotel and hostel, sightseeing, swimming on the last day.
kids.d: Credit questions about rural travel, unwell contacts, animals or medical care overseas.

kids.x: Pre-travel vaccines and prophylaxis: childhood vaccines only, nothing before the trip.

check.x: Asks about her last menstrual period (last week) or whether she could be pregnant.
Takes the past medical, medication and allergy history: asthma since age 5, no gallstones or cancer; Ventolin with no recent changes; no allergies.
Takes a family history: no hepatitis, gallstones or cancer.
Takes a social history: non-smoker, lives with her boyfriend in a city apartment, interior designer, born in Australia.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: unsure of the cause, scared, wants to know what is going on.
Examination
Asks for vital signs and identifies the low-grade fever (37.8 °C) with otherwise normal observations.
Inspects for jaundice in the sclerae and the skin, and notes the scratch marks.
Looks for signs of liver failure and chronic liver disease: confusion and asterixis (encephalopathy), bruising, spider naevi, palmar erythema, leuconychia and ascites.
check.d: Encephalopathy (mental state or asterixis) must be checked for the item.

check.x: Examines the abdomen: right upper quadrant tenderness, a smooth tender liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, Murphy's sign, the spleen and shifting dullness.
Requests a urine dipstick (bilirubin 2+) and a urine pregnancy test (negative).
Interpretation
Interprets the hepatitis A serology: a positive HAV IgM means acute or recent hepatitis A infection.
Interprets the hepatitis B and C serology: HBsAg and anti-HBc negative with anti-HBs positive means immunity from vaccination, not infection; anti-HCV negative.

Interprets the liver tests as a hepatocellular picture: ALT 853 and AST 334 markedly raised (ALT about 24 times the upper limit), with only a mild rise in ALP and GGT; a high, mainly conjugated bilirubin of 88 explains the jaundice, dark urine and pale stools.
States that liver synthetic function is preserved (INR 1.1, albumin 45), so there is no sign of acute liver failure.
Interprets the FBC: normal haemoglobin and platelets argue against haemolysis or malaria, and a normal white cell count argues against cholangitis; the mildly raised CRP fits viral hepatitis.
Interprets the ultrasound: no gallstones and no bile duct dilatation, so there is no biliary obstruction; mild hepatomegaly and gallbladder wall thickening fit acute hepatitis.

Gives acute hepatitis A as the most likely diagnosis and justifies it: returned traveller who ate street food without pre-travel vaccination, a prodrome followed by jaundice, a hepatocellular picture and a positive HAV IgM.
Gives differentials, each with a feature for or against:
check.d: Credit other reasonable differentials (for example leptospirosis after swimming, or EBV) given with a feature for or against.

kids.x: Ascending cholangitis or choledocholithiasis: fever, RUQ pain and jaundice; against: no stones or duct dilatation, hepatocellular picture, normal white cell count.
Drug-induced or autoimmune hepatitis: against: no new medicines or herbal products, and a positive HAV IgM explains the picture.
Malaria: for: fever within 3 months of travel to South-East Asia; against: normal platelets and haemoglobin, and HAV IgM explains the picture.
kids.d: Credit requesting thick and thin films or a malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT) if there was any rural or border-area travel or the fever persists.

kids.x: Hepatitis E: for: enteric exposure in Asia, clinically identical to hepatitis A; against: only the positive HAV IgM (pregnancy test negative, so lower risk of severe disease).

check.x: Management
Explains the diagnosis in plain words: a virus caught from contaminated food or water that inflames the liver; most people recover fully within weeks, and it does not become a long-term infection.
Plans supportive care at home: rest, fluids, small frequent meals, no alcohol, and no new medicines (including over-the-counter or herbal products) without checking with the GP.
Notifies the local public health unit, because hepatitis A is a notifiable disease.
Advises handwashing and not preparing food for others until a week after jaundice onset, and that she can return to her non-food-handling work when well.

Arranges protection for her partner, a close household and sexual contact: hepatitis A vaccine (or normal human immunoglobulin if the public health unit advises it) as soon as possible and within 2 weeks of the last exposure (exposure is ongoing, so give it now).
Offers an STI screen (she has never had one).
Safety netting

Tells her to go to the ED (or call 000 if severe) for confusion or drowsiness, unusual bruising or bleeding, vomiting so that she cannot keep fluids down, severe or worsening abdominal pain, rapidly deepening jaundice, or high fevers with shaking.
check.d: Award for at least three red flags in plain words, linked to the ED or 000. Optional extra credit: advises seeing the GP sooner if she is not improving, is not eating or the itch is unbearable.

check.x: Plans monitoring and follow-up: repeat LFTs and INR within a few days and then until they return to normal; refers her to the ED or hepatology if the INR rises (1.5 or more), she becomes confused or drowsy, or she cannot keep fluids down; and gives written information.
check.d: Credit whether given in the management or the safety-netting answer.

part2.lead: At the end of your first consultation Sanjana had blood tests and an abdominal ultrasound. She has come back two days later for the results. Here they are.
part2.patient:
Ask each question once, and only if the candidate has not already covered it while explaining the plan:

  • "Is my boyfriend going to catch it?"
  • "Will this damage my liver for good?"
  • "Can I go back to work?"

You are relieved to have an answer. If the candidate uses jargon such as "transaminases", "notifiable" or "post-exposure prophylaxis" without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: Hepatitis serology
handover.model:
• Read, marker by marker: HAV IgM positive means a recent hepatitis A infection (total anti-HAV is positive as well). HBsAg negative means there is no current hepatitis B infection. Anti-HBs positive with anti-HBc negative means immunity from vaccination: natural infection would make anti-HBc positive too. Anti-HCV negative.
  • For Sanjana: acute hepatitis A, which fits street food in Thailand without pre-travel vaccination and an incubation period of about a month. Her hepatitis B immunity probably comes from vaccination in childhood or at school.
  • What it changes: notify the public health unit, give infection-control advice, and arrange vaccination for her partner. Hepatitis A does not become chronic, so the focus is supportive care and watching for liver failure.

handover.label: Blood tests
handover.model:
• Read: ALT 853 (about 24 times the upper limit) and AST 334 are markedly raised. ALP 178 and GGT 68 are only mildly raised, so this is a hepatocellular pattern with a small cholestatic component. Bilirubin 88, mostly conjugated (66). Albumin 45 and INR 1.1 are normal. FBC normal. Creatinine normal. CRP mildly raised at 9.
  • For Sanjana: acute hepatocellular injury, which fits viral hepatitis. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia explains the jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and itch. Synthetic function is preserved, so there is no acute liver failure. A normal haemoglobin argues against haemolysis or malaria, and normal white cells argue against cholangitis.
  • What it changes: she can be managed at home. The INR is the key result to repeat, because a rising INR or any encephalopathy means acute liver failure and urgent hospital care.

handover.label: Abdominal ultrasound
handover.result:
Examination: ultrasound of the upper abdomen (liver, biliary tree, pancreas, spleen and kidneys).

Clinical details: 30-year-old woman with 2 weeks of fever, malaise and RUQ pain, now jaundiced with dark urine and pale stools. Returned from Thailand one month ago. Query biliary obstruction.

Findings:

  • Liver: mildly enlarged at 16.5 cm in the midclavicular line, with a smooth outline. The parenchyma is diffusely slightly hypoechoic, with prominent echogenic portal venule walls. No focal lesion.
  • Gallbladder: partly contracted, with diffuse wall thickening of 5 mm. No gallstones or sludge. No pericholecystic fluid. Sonographic Murphy's sign negative.
  • Bile ducts: common bile duct 4 mm. No intrahepatic duct dilatation.
  • Portal vein: patent, with flow towards the liver.
  • Pancreas: normal where seen.
  • Spleen: normal size (11 cm).
  • Kidneys: normal.
  • Ascites: none.

Conclusion: no gallstones and no biliary dilatation. Mild hepatomegaly with diffuse parenchymal change and gallbladder wall thickening, in keeping with acute hepatitis. No features of chronic liver disease.
handover.model:
• Read: no gallstones, a normal-calibre common bile duct and no intrahepatic duct dilatation. Mildly enlarged liver with diffuse change and no focal lesion. Gallbladder wall thickening without stones, pericholecystic fluid or a sonographic Murphy's sign. Normal spleen, patent portal vein, no ascites.
  • For Sanjana: no biliary obstruction, so the jaundice is hepatic, not post-hepatic. This makes choledocholithiasis and cholangitis very unlikely. Gallbladder wall thickening is common in acute hepatitis and is not acute cholecystitis here (no stones, Murphy's negative). There is no sign of chronic liver disease or portal hypertension.
  • What it changes: no ERCP or surgical referral is needed. Management is that of acute viral hepatitis.

ask: You are now presenting Sanjana to your supervising GP. Please give an ISBAR handover of Sanjana Kumar, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Sanjana now, here in general practice.
Before Sanjana goes home, what would you tell her and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self (medical student); Sanjana Kumar, 30.
  • Situation: jaundice from acute hepatitis A; well, with no liver failure.
  • Background: 2 weeks of feeling hot, anorexia, malaise, constant RUQ pain, dark urine, pale stools, itch, nausea. Back from Thailand a month ago, ate street food, no pre-travel vaccines. No alcohol or blood-borne risks; asthma, Ventolin only.
  • Assessment: HAV IgM positive: acute hepatitis A. Anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc negative: hepatitis B vaccine-immune; HCV negative. ALT 853, AST 334, mild ALP and GGT rise: hepatocellular. Bilirubin 88, mostly conjugated. INR 1.1, albumin 45: synthetic function preserved. FBC normal. Ultrasound: no stones or duct dilatation.
  • Recommendation: supportive care at home, notify public health, vaccinate her partner, repeat LFTs and INR within a few days.

Most likely: acute hepatitis A. Returned from Thailand a month ago, ate street food, no pre-travel vaccines; prodrome then jaundice; hepatocellular LFTs; HAV IgM positive.

  • Ascending cholangitis or choledocholithiasis: for: fever, RUQ pain, jaundice, pale stools. Against: no stones or duct dilatation, ALT far above ALP, normal white cells.
  • Drug-induced or autoimmune hepatitis: for: hepatocellular picture in a young woman. Against: no new medicines or herbal products, and the HAV IgM explains it.
  • Malaria: for: fever within 3 months of travel to South-East Asia. Against: normal haemoglobin and platelets, and the HAV IgM explains the picture. Thick and thin films or an RDT if any rural or border-area travel or the fever persists.
  • Hepatitis E: for: enteric exposure in Asia; clinically identical to hepatitis A. Against: only the positive HAV IgM; pregnancy test negative, so lower risk of severe disease. (Acute hepatitis B is excluded: HBsAg and anti-HBc negative.)

1. Explain: a food- or water-borne virus inflaming the liver; most people recover fully and it does not become chronic.
  2. Supportive care at home: rest, fluids, small frequent meals, no alcohol, no new medicines or herbal products without checking.
  3. Notify the local public health unit (notifiable disease).
  4. Prevent spread: handwashing and no preparing food for others until a week after jaundice onset; she can return to her design work (not food handling) when well.
  5. Partner: hepatitis A vaccine (or immunoglobulin if public health advises) as soon as possible and within 2 weeks of the last exposure (exposure is ongoing, so give it now).
  6. Offer an STI screen.

Go to the ED (call 000 if severe) for:

  • confusion, drowsiness or behaving strangely
  • unusual bruising or bleeding
  • vomiting so that she can't keep fluids down
  • severe or worsening tummy pain, or jaundice getting rapidly deeper
  • high fevers with shaking

See the GP sooner (optional credit) if she is not improving, cannot eat, or the itch is unbearable.

Follow-up: GP review with repeat LFTs and INR within a few days, then until the liver tests are normal; ED or hepatology if the INR is 1.5 or more, she becomes confused, or she cannot keep fluids down. Confirm the public health notification and her partner's vaccination. Give written information on hepatitis A.

ddx.for: Returned from Thailand a month ago after eating street food without pre-travel vaccination, with a 2-week prodrome, then jaundice, a hepatocellular picture and a positive HAV IgM.
Fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice (Charcot's triad), with pale stools and dark urine.
ddx.against: No gallstones or bile duct dilatation on ultrasound, ALT far higher than ALP, and a normal white cell count.

ddx.dx: Choledocholithiasis (gallstone obstruction of the bile duct)
ddx.for: Right upper quadrant pain, pale stools, dark urine and itch.
ddx.against: Constant pain not related to food, no history of gallstones, and no stones or duct dilatation on ultrasound.

ddx.for: Fever within 3 months of returning from South-East Asia.
ddx.against: Normal haemoglobin and platelets, and a positive HAV IgM explains the picture.

ddx.for: Hepatocellular liver injury in a young woman.
ddx.against: Takes only Ventolin with no recent changes or herbal products, and a positive HAV IgM explains the picture.

ddx.dx: Other acute viral hepatitis (hepatitis E or acute hepatitis B)
ddx.for: Enteric exposures in Asia and an acute hepatitic illness clinically identical to hepatitis A.
ddx.against: Only the positive HAV IgM argues against hepatitis E; HBsAg and anti-HBc are negative with vaccine-type anti-HBs, which excludes acute hepatitis B.

guide:
This is a general practice station, so there is no observation chart: give the observations from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them. In Part 1 the examiner gives examination findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The patient answers only what is asked; anything not in the script is "no" or "I don't know". If the candidate asks for tests in Part 1, say the results will come in Part 2, but give the urine dipstick and pregnancy test from the Exam findings if they are requested. In Part 2 hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order, allowing about 75 seconds for each. Sanjana asks each of her questions only if the candidate has not already covered it.

The source case gives marks for exploring differentials from at least three systems and for constitutional symptoms. Credit questions that test pre-hepatic, hepatic and post-hepatic causes, and a structured returned-traveller history.

A high-performing candidate asks about the 4 Ps (pee, poo, pruritus, pain), constitutional symptoms, blood-borne and sexual risk factors, alcohol and medicines, and takes a full travel history, finding the street food and the missing pre-travel vaccines. They examine for encephalopathy and chronic liver disease as well as the tender liver. In Part 2 they read HAV IgM as acute hepatitis A and anti-HBs alone as vaccine immunity, call the LFTs hepatocellular with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, notice the normal INR, notify public health, protect her partner and set clear INR-based escalation criteria.

A borderline candidate takes a generic history without the travel or vaccine questions, misreads anti-HBs as hepatitis B infection, calls the picture obstructive, overlooks notification or her partner, or gives no plan to recheck the INR.
explain:
Diagnosis

Sanjana has acute hepatitis A. She returned from Thailand a month ago after eating street food without hepatitis A vaccination, which fits the incubation period of about 2 to 7 weeks (usually around 4). She had a two-week prodrome of feeling hot, anorexia, malaise and nausea, then right upper quadrant pain, dark urine, pale stools, itch and jaundice. The tender, mildly enlarged liver, a hepatocellular rise in liver enzymes and a positive HAV IgM confirm it.

An approach to jaundice

  • Pre-hepatic (unconjugated): Gilbert's syndrome, haemolysis, thalassaemia, sickle cell disease, malaria, G6PD deficiency.
  • Hepatic: viral, alcoholic, autoimmune or drug-induced hepatitis, NAFLD, liver cancer.
  • Post-hepatic (conjugated, obstructive): gallstones, pancreatic head tumour, cholangiocarcinoma, cholangitis, primary biliary cholangitis, stricture.

Dark urine and pale stools mean conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia: conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and passes into the urine, and less reaches the gut. Always ask the 4 Ps (pee, poo, pruritus, pain), the hepatitis risk factors (injecting drugs, tattoos, piercings, transfusions, needlesticks, sexual history, alcohol, medicines and herbal products) and, in a returned traveller, accommodation, food and drink, rural travel, vaccines and prophylaxis, unwell contacts, medical care overseas and animal or water exposure.

Interpreting the results

  • Hepatitis serology: HBsAg means hepatitis B infection (acute or chronic). HBeAg means active replication. Anti-HBs means immunity, from infection or vaccination. Anti-HBc means past or current infection. HAV IgM means recent hepatitis A. Sanjana's pattern (anti-HBs positive, HBsAg and anti-HBc negative) is vaccine immunity, and the positive HAV IgM is the diagnosis.
  • Liver tests: transaminases far more raised than ALP and GGT give a hepatocellular pattern. ALT above AST is typical of viral hepatitis. The mild ALP and GGT rise reflects the cholestatic phase of hepatitis A. Normal albumin and INR show preserved synthetic function. The INR is the best early marker of liver failure.
  • FBC: a normal haemoglobin argues against haemolysis, and normal white cells argue against cholangitis.
  • Ultrasound: excludes biliary obstruction. Gallbladder wall thickening is a recognised finding in acute hepatitis and does not mean cholecystitis without stones or a sonographic Murphy's sign.

Differentials that matter

  • Ascending cholangitis (fever, RUQ pain and jaundice) is a must-not-miss diagnosis, and so is choledocholithiasis. The ultrasound and the enzyme pattern exclude them here.
  • Drug-induced and autoimmune hepatitis are other hepatic causes. Ask about all medicines and herbal products.
  • Travel infections: exclude malaria in a febrile traveller from an endemic area when the picture is not explained (thick and thin films or a rapid diagnostic test). Think of hepatitis E after enteric exposure in Asia: it is clinically identical to hepatitis A and only serology separates them, and it can be severe in pregnancy (her period was last week and her pregnancy test is negative). Consider leptospirosis after freshwater exposure.

Hepatitis A

Hepatitis A spreads by the faecal-oral route, through contaminated food and water or close contact (including sexual contact). People are most infectious in the 2 weeks before jaundice and remain infectious until about a week after it starts. It does not cause chronic infection. Most adults recover fully within weeks, although symptoms and abnormal LFTs can persist or relapse. Fulminant hepatitis is rare and more likely with older age or pre-existing liver disease.

Management

  • Supportive care: rest, fluids and nutrition. No alcohol, and avoid medicines that can harm the liver: check any new medicine, including over-the-counter and herbal products.
  • Monitoring: repeat LFTs and INR until they normalise. A rising INR, encephalopathy, or vomiting that stops her keeping fluids down needs hospital assessment and hepatology input.
  • Public health (CDNA Series of National Guidelines: Hepatitis A): hepatitis A is notifiable. Give hygiene advice: careful handwashing after the toilet and before food, no preparing food for others, separate towels, and avoiding sex while infectious. Food handlers, childcare workers and healthcare workers are excluded from work until a week after jaundice onset. The public health unit identifies contacts.
  • Contacts (Australian Immunisation Handbook): post-exposure prophylaxis as soon as possible and within 2 weeks of the last exposure; her partner's exposure is ongoing, so give it now. Hepatitis A vaccine is used for most contacts aged 12 months or older, and normal human immunoglobulin for some groups, as the public health unit advises. Her partner is a household and sexual contact.
  • Prevention: hepatitis A vaccine is recommended before travel to countries where hepatitis A is common. After this infection she will be immune for life. Offer the STI screen she has never had.

Safety netting

She should go to the ED for confusion or drowsiness, bruising or bleeding, persistent vomiting, worsening pain or deepening jaundice, or high fevers with rigors. Book GP review with repeat LFTs and INR within a few days, then continue until the liver tests are normal.
points: Dark urine and pale stools mean conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Always ask the 4 Ps (pee, poo, pruritus, pain) in jaundice.
A returned traveller with jaundice needs a structured travel history: food and water, accommodation, activities, rural travel, contacts, medical care overseas, and pre-travel vaccines.
HAV IgM positive means acute hepatitis A. Anti-HBs positive with anti-HBc negative means hepatitis B immunity from vaccination, not infection.
Transaminases far higher than ALP and GGT give a hepatocellular pattern. INR and mental state are the markers of acute liver failure and decide who needs hospital.

Hepatitis A is notifiable: give hygiene advice, exclude food handlers, childcare and healthcare workers for a week after jaundice onset, and give close contacts post-exposure prophylaxis as soon as possible and within 2 weeks of the last exposure.
Fever, RUQ pain and jaundice should prompt you to exclude cholangitis, and fever after travel should prompt you to consider malaria.
